verdict.reasoning: Patient reports urinary pain and frequency for just under a week: "it's been going on for a few days now" and later "it's been going on for a little bit longer than three days... about just under a week"; dysuria is described as "it hurts when I kind of pee" and increased frequency as "I'm going to the toilet a lot more".
Same as cc-001: dysuria ("it hurts when I kind of pee" / "burning stinging when I go to the toilet") and increased frequency ("going to the toilet a lot more") for "about just under a week."

Patient reports pink urine today: "today I noticed it was like a bit pink" and "I think it was mixed in, probably. I don't know, it was pink." Interpreting this as possible hematuria is a direct clinical inference.

She describes lower abdominal pain at the bottom of her tummy, worse on voiding, without radiation: "it's kind of at the bottom of my tummy mainly when I go to the loo... An achy pain, I suppose" and when asked if it moves to back or sides: "No. No." Dull/achy suprapubic pain is a reasonable synonym.

Transcript documents denial of nausea and vomiting ("Any other symptoms... nausea, vomiting?" "No."), and no noticed fevers ("Any temperatures or fevers?" "No, no, not that I've noticed."). Flank/back pain are not asked or denied; only radiation of tummy pain to back/sides is queried. The explicit denial of back/flank pain as systemic red flags is not fully documented, so including them as denied adds information.

She has baseline IBS with variable stool consistency and no change: "I usually have a bit of problems with my bowels anyway"; "I think I have ibs... sometimes it's a bit softer, sometimes it's bit... hard to predict"; and "you've noticed no new symptoms?... No, no".
Doctor asks "When was your last period?" and patient replies "Two weeks ago."
She is sexually active with a long-term boyfriend and they generally do not use condoms: "Yeah, I have a long term boyfriend"; "I guess because I don't really use condoms with my boyfriend."
She confirms use of a combined oral contraceptive: "Yeah, I'm on the pill" and when asked "combined pill or the mini pill?" she answers "Combined pill."
History of IBS: patient states "I think I have ibs" and doctor later: "any other medical conditions apart from the ibs?"
Medication list includes combined oral contraceptive: "Yeah, I'm on the pill" and clarified as "Combined pill."
She takes mebeverine: "Apart from the pill, I take something for the IBS as well. It begins with an M... Like mebbe. Something." Doctor: "Yeah... that's it." This refers to mebeverine.

Doctor states treatment choice: "we've got choice to antibiotics, something called trimethoprin or nitrofurantoin, which is a three day course normally." This is a plan to start a 3‑day course of one of these for presumed UTI.
Analgesia advice given: "If you are having some pain, simple paracetamol would probably be advisable."
Allergy to clindamycin noted: "there was an antibiotic called Clindus, Clindamycin... that didn't go too well right with me." Reaction is not specified further.
No family history of bladder or kidney disease: doctor asks "any history of problems with the bladder or the kidneys?" patient: "No."
Cannabis use timing: "I smoked weed for the first time like a week and a half ago."
Alcohol use: "I drink occasionally socially with friends."
She denies smoking tobacco: "I tried weed the first time, but I don't smoke."
Living situation and being a student: "I am living in halls at the moment, uni" and later "I'm studying English."

Doctor advises avoiding cannabis: "I do strongly advise you to... make it a regular habit if you can" (clearly meaning avoid use) and later "I would strongly recommend you to avoid as you can." This constitutes counseling to avoid cannabis.

There is no discussion in the transcript of reinforcing safe sex practices or adherence to the pill; contraception is only fact-finding (type of pill, unprotected sex) and pregnancy risk, without explicit behavioral counseling.

Doctor’s assessment: "I think it's probably just a simple, what we say, UTI or cystitis, bladder infection" and notes absence of systemic features: "you haven't got any other symptoms that suggest... things like fevers and back pain would be more worrying." Symptoms described include dysuria, frequency, and pink urine suggesting mild hematuria.

IBS is chronic and unchanged: she describes longstanding IBS and confirms no new bowel symptoms: "I think I have ibs"; "you've noticed no new symptoms?... No." This supports assessment as stable chronic IBS.

Plan for MSU/dip and culture: "it's probably worth giving us a urine sample... which we can test there and then with a urine dip and send it off to the lab." That is a mid-stream urine for dipstick and culture.
Treatment plan: "we've got choice to antibiotics, something called trimethoprin or nitrofurantoin, which is a three day course normally."
Supportive measures: "make sure you're well hydrated, drink plenty of fluids. If you are having some pain, simple paracetamol would probably be advisable."

Safety-netting: "Do bear in mind those symptoms I mentioned about the fever and the back pain and vomiting. If you have any of those, give me a call." and earlier: "if things are still any better next week, come back and see me and we can have another look again" (intended as if not better next week).
There is no explicit plan stated about IBS or continuing mebeverine; IBS is only taken as background history and current medication, without management advice.
No advice is given regarding diet or IBS management in the transcript.
Lifestyle counseling to avoid cannabis is given: "I do strongly advise you to... [not] make it a regular habit" and "I would strongly recommend you to avoid as you can."
There is no counseling recorded on safe sex practices or adherence to the oral contraceptive; discussion is limited to assessing pregnancy risk and current contraception.
Doctor notes "at this age, I wouldn't normally examine you" and no physical examination or vital signs are described anywhere in the transcript, so absence of documented findings is accurate.
